claim: The first mitochondrial fusion gene, fuzzy onions (fzo), was discovered in 1997 in a Drosophila melanogaster mutant exhibiting male sterility.
source: The first mitochondrial fusion gene, fuzzy onions (fzo), was discovered in 1997 in a Drosophila melanogaster mutant exhibiting male sterility (Hales and Fuller, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hales and Fuller, 1997

claim: During early spermatid development in flies, mitochondria aggregate and fuse to become two giant organelles that wrap around each other to form the Nebenkern.
source: During early spermatid development in flies, mitochondria aggregate and fuse to become two giant organelles that wrap around each other to form the Nebenkern (Fuller, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuller, 1993

claim: Mutations in fzo abolish mitochondrial fusion in spermatids, resulting in a morphologically aberrant Nebenkern and sterility.
source: Mutations in fzo abolish mitochondrial fusion in spermatids, resulting in a morphologically aberrant Nebenkern and sterility.
evidence: Follows from the description of fzo discovery and its role in mitochondrial fusion

claim: In humans, there are two mitofusin homologs known as MFN1 and MFN2.
source: In humans, there are two homologs known as MFN1 and MFN2 (Santel and Fuller, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santel and Fuller, 2001

claim: Fusion acts as a major quality control mechanism for mitochondria by enabling mixing of matrix components and promoting their homogenization.
source: Fusion acts as a major quality control mechanism for mitochondria by enabling mixing of matrix components and promoting their homogenization (Chan, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan, 2012

claim: In the absence of fusion, mitochondria diverge, become functionally heterogenous, and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) are diminished.
source: In the absence of fusion, mitochondria diverge, become functionally heterogenous, and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) are diminished (Chen et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2010; Weaver et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Chen et al. and Weaver et al.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion affects mitochondrial transport and degradation.
source: Mitochondrial fusion also affects mitochondrial transport and degradation (Chen et al., 2003; Gomes et al., 2011; Kandul et al., 2016; Misko et al., 2010; Rambold et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Spermatogenesis is a cyclical process that involves differentiation of spermatogonia into spermatocytes, which undergo meiosis to form haploid spermatids and ultimately spermatozoa.
source: In mammals, spermatogenesis is a cyclical process that involves differentiation of spermatogonia into spermatocytes, which undergo meiosis to form haploid spermatids and ultimately spermatozoa (Griswold, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Griswold, 2016

claim: Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier (BTB) that separates the seminiferous epithelium into the basal and apical compartments.
source: In addition to providing differentiation cues and metabolites for the developing germ cells, Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier (BTB) that separates the seminiferous epithelium into the basal (towards the periphery) and apical (towards the lumen) compartments (Stanton, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stanton, 2016

claim: Some patients with mtDNA disease have sperm defects.
source: Some patients with mtDNA disease have sperm defects (Demain et al., 2017; Folgerø et al., 1993), and sperm from some infertile males harbor mtDNA mutations (Baklouti-Gargouri et al., 2014; Carra et al., 2004; Kao et al., 1995; Lestienne et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Mouse models with a pathogenic mtDNA deletion exhibit spermatogenic arrest during the zygotene stage of Meiotic Prophase I (MPI).
source: Mouse models with a pathogenic mtDNA deletion exhibit spermatogenic arrest during the zygotene stage of Meiotic Prophase I (MPI) (Nakada et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakada et al., 2006

claim: A mouse model that is unable to utilize mitochondrial ATP exhibits spermatogenic arrest during the leptotene stage of MPI.
source: Furthermore, a mouse model that is unable to utilize mitochondrial ATP exhibits spermatogenic arrest during the leptotene stage of MPI (Brower et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brower et al., 2009

claim: Mouse models that accumulate mtDNA mutations exhibit male infertility.
source: Finally, mouse models that accumulate mtDNA mutations exhibit male infertility (Jiang et al., 2017; Kujoth et al., 2005; Trifunovic et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The Drosophila homolog of mitofusin (dMfn) regulates lipid homeostasis and maintenance of germline stem cells in the testis.
source: The Drosophila homolog of mitofusin (dMfn) was recently shown to regulate lipid homeostasis and maintenance of germline stem cells in the testis (Sênos Demarco et al., 2019),
evidence: Supported by citation to Sênos Demarco et al., 2019

claim: Low Mfn2 expression in sperm is associated with asthenozoospermia (reduced sperm motility) and reduced sperm mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: A clinical study found that low Mfn2 expression in sperm is associated with asthenozoospermia (reduced sperm motility) and reduced sperm mitochondrial membrane potential (Fang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fang et al., 2018

claim: Mfn1 is required for spermatogenesis in the mouse.
source: Finally, Mfn1 is required for spermatogenesis in the mouse (Zhang et al., 2016), but the precise stage of the defect as well as the role of Mfn2 remain unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016

claim: Stra8-Cre expression begins at post-natal day 3 (P3) in undifferentiated spermatogonia.
source: Stra8-Cre expression is reported to begin at post-natal day 3 (P3) in undifferentiated spermatogonia (Sadate-Ngatchou et al., 2008), including the majority of early stem-like GFRα1-positive spermatogonia (Hobbs et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sadate-Ngatchou et al., 2008 and Hobbs et al., 2015

claim: All three mitofusin-deficient mouse lines (S8::Mfn1, S8::Mfn2, and S8::Dm) were healthy and showed no changes in weight.
source: All three mitofusin-deficient mouse lines were healthy and showed no changes in weight (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Mitofusin-deficient mice had obviously smaller testes compared with controls.
source: However, they had obviously smaller testes compared with controls (Figure 1A and B), suggesting an essential role for mitochondrial fusion during spermatogenesis.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: There is significant reduction of spermatozoa in the epididymides of S8::Mfn1 and S8::Mfn2 mice, with the defect more severe with loss of Mfn1.
source: Indeed, there is significant reduction of spermatozoa in the epididymides of S8::Mfn1 and S8::Mfn2 mice, with the defect more severe with loss of Mfn1 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: Residual spermatozoa in S8::Mfn1 and S8::Mfn2 mutants often display mitochondrial fragmentation and reduced mitochondrial content.
source: The residual spermatozoa in both mutant lines often display mitochondrial fragmentation and reduced mitochondrial content (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E and F

claim: Mutant spermatozoa exhibit morphological defects, particularly kinking near or in the midpiece.
source: Mutant spermatozoa also exhibit morphological defects, particularly kinking near or in the midpiece (Figure 1E and G), and almost a complete loss of motility (Figure 1H; Videos 1–3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E, G, H and Videos 1-3

claim: S8::Dm mice have a complete absence of epididymal spermatozoa.
source: S8::Dm mice have the smallest testes (Figure 1A and B) and strikingly, a complete absence of epididymal spermatozoa (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A, B, C, and D

claim: At P24, mutant mice have substantially smaller testes compared with control.
source: Even at this early time point, mutant mice have substantially smaller testes compared with control (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Mutant seminiferous tubules are narrower in diameter, sparsely populated, and contain numerous Sertoli cell vacuolizations.
source: We performed Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) staining in testis sections and found that mutant seminiferous tubules are narrower in diameter, sparsely populated, and contain numerous Sertoli cell vacuolizations (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: S8::Dm tubules have almost a complete absence of post-meiotic spermatids, indicative of an inability to complete meiosis.
source: Whereas most control seminiferous tubules are packed with round spermatids, S8::Dm tubules have almost a complete absence of post-meiotic spermatids, indicative of an inability to complete meiosis.
evidence: Based on histological analysis described in the text

claim: The majority of control seminiferous tubules (87 ± 6%) at P24 contained germ cells differentiated up to the spermatid stage.
source: As expected for the P24 time point, the majority of control seminiferous tubules (87 ± 6%) contained germ cells differentiated up to the spermatid stage, and the remaining tubules (13 ± 6%) contained cells differentiated up to pachytene/diplotene.
evidence: Quantitative data from analysis of testis sections

claim: The majority of seminiferous tubules from P24 S8::Dm mice contained cells differentiated only up to the leptotene/zygotene stage (55 ± 2%), indicating a meiotic defect during early MPI.
source: In contrast, the majority of seminiferous tubules from P24 S8::Dm mice contained cells differentiated only up to the leptotene/zygotene stage (55 ± 2%), indicating a meiotic defect during early MPI.
evidence: Quantitative data from analysis of testis sections

claim: S8::Dm mice have a reduction of pachytene and diplotene spermatocytes and an abundance of both leptotene and zygotene cells, pinpointing the meiotic defect to the zygotene-to-pachytene transition.
source: Consistent with data from testis sections, we found that S8::Dm mice have a reduction of pachytene and diplotene spermatocytes and an abundance of both leptotene and zygotene cells, pinpointing the meiotic defect to the zygotene-to-pachytene transition (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2G from chromosomal spreading analysis

claim: Loss of Mfn1 alone was sufficient to cause a similar defect in meiosis, resulting in accumulation of spermatocytes in the leptotene and zygotene stages, and reduced production of spermatids.
source: We found that loss of Mfn1 alone was sufficient to cause a similar defect in meiosis, resulting in accumulation of spermatocytes in the leptotene and zygotene stages, and reduced production of spermatids.
evidence: Based on histology and chromosomal spreading in S8::Mfn1 mice

claim: S8::Mfn2 mice had normal progression through MPI at P24.
source: In contrast, S8::Mfn2 mice had normal progression through MPI at P24.
evidence: Based on histology and chromosomal spreading in S8::Mfn2 mice

claim: MPI is the most sensitive stage of spermatogenesis to disruption of mitochondrial fusion.
source: Because Stra8-Cre-mediated excision occurs in all germ cell types, including spermatogonia that give rise to meiotic spermatocytes, our results demonstrate that MPI is the most sensitive stage of spermatogenesis to disruption of mitochondrial fusion (Figure 2H).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and shown in Figure 2H

claim: In P24 WT mice, pachytene/diplotene cells contained over three times more mitochondrial signal compared with leptotene/zygotene spermatocytes.
source: In P24 WT mice, we found that pachytene/diplotene cells contained over three times more mitochondrial signal compared with leptotene/zygotene spermatocytes (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: Pachytene/diplotene spermatocytes in S8::Dm mutant animals have less than half the mitochondrial content found in WT animals.
source: Pachytene/diplotene spermatocytes are much sparser in S8::Dm mutant animals, but when present, these cells have less than half the mitochondrial content found in WT animals (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B

claim: WT pachytene/diplotene spermatocytes, compared with leptotene/zygotene spermatocytes, contain elongated and highly clustered mitochondria.
source: We found that WT pachytene/diplotene spermatocytes, compared with leptotene/zygotene spermatocytes, contain elongated and highly clustered mitochondria (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C and D from meiotic spreading

claim: S8::Dm spermatocytes that reach the pachytene/diplotene stage have less mitochondrial content and their mitochondria are more fragmented.
source: Furthermore, S8::Dm spermatocytes that do make it to the pachytene/diplotene stage have less mitochondrial content and their mitochondria are more fragmented (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C and D

claim: Pachytene/diplotene spermatocytes have strong expression of MPC1, while spermatogonia have little to no MPC1 protein.
source: Indeed, we find that while pachytene/diplotene spermatocytes have strong expression of MPC1, spermatogonia have little to no MPC1 protein (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Compared with diploid spermatogonia, tetraploid spermatocytes have substantially greater maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity, and a modest increase in basal respiration and ATP production.
source: Indeed, compared with diploid spermatogonia, tetraploid spermatocytes have substantially greater maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity, and a modest increase in basal respiration and ATP production (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: By P56, the testes of S8::Dm mice have undergone repeated rounds of spermatogenesis and show greater germ cell depletion and more widespread Sertoli cell vacuolization compared with P24 mutants.
source: By this time, the testes have undergone repeated rounds of spermatogenesis and should have more complete depletion of mitofusins. PAS-stained testis sections from P56 S8::Dm mice showed greater germ cell depletion and more widespread Sertoli cell vacuolization (Figure 4A) compared with P24 mutants.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Flow cytometry showed an 80% loss of mito-Dendra2-positive cells from dissociated S8::Dm testes compared with control at P56.
source: This severe depletion of germ cells was confirmed by flow cytometry, which showed an 80% loss of mito-Dendra2-positive cells from dissociated S8::Dm testes compared with control (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: Nearly half of the P56 mutant tubules (48 ± 7%) contain only spermatogonia.
source: Whereas WT seminiferous tubules invariably contain spermatids at this age, nearly half of the P56 mutant tubules (48 ± 7%) contain only spermatogonia (Figure 4D and E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4D, E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: S8::Dm tubules, compared with WT, had greater than 80% depletion of all differentiating germ cell types at P56.
source: Consistent with the flow cytometry data, quantification using molecular markers showed that S8::Dm tubules, compared with WT, had greater than 80% depletion of all differentiating germ cell types (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Mutant seminiferous tubules retained an outer rim of mito-Dendra2-positive germ cells that stained with PLZF, a marker of undifferentiated spermatogonia.
source: Despite this severe depletion of germ cells, mutant seminiferous tubules retained an outer rim of mito-Dendra2-positive germ cells that stained with PLZF, a marker of undifferentiated spermatogonia (Figure 4A and D rightmost panel, and 4F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A, D, and F

claim: GFRα1-positive spermatogonia were present in S8::Dm mice, and their numbers were increased over 50%.
source: Not only were GFRα1-positive spermatogonia present in S8::Dm mice, their numbers were increased over 50%.
evidence: Based on quantification from testis sections

claim: The vast majority of GFRα1-positive spermatogonia express Stra8-Cre/Dn in WT and S8::Dm mice.
source: Quantification from testis sections in WT and S8::Dm mice shows that the vast majority of GFRα1-positive spermatogonia express Stra8-Cre/Dn (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Over 40% of GFRα1-expressing spermatogonia are positive for the proliferation marker Ki-67, similar to that in WT animals.
source: Furthermore, over 40% of these GFRα1-expressing spermatogonia are positive for the proliferation marker Ki-67, similar to that in WT animals (Figure 4H and I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4H and I

claim: Even in P116 mice, mutant seminiferous tubules retain an outer rim of undifferentiated spermatogonia that stain with Ki-67.
source: Even in these older mice, mutant seminiferous tubules retain an outer rim of undifferentiated spermatogonia that stain with Ki-67 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Loss of either Mfn1 or Mfn2 alone causes severe depletion of germ cells.
source: As in S8::Dm mice, loss of either Mfn1 or Mfn2 alone causes severe depletion of germ cells.
evidence: Based on histology in S8::Mfn1 and S8::Mfn2 mice

claim: Both Mfn1 and Mfn2 are required for maintenance of differentiating spermatogonia.
source: Quantification of c-Kit-expressing spermatogonia showed that both mutants have severe depletion of differentiating spermatogonia, close to the level observed in S8::Dm mice. Thus, both Mfn1 and Mfn2 are required for maintenance of differentiating spermatogonia.
evidence: Based on quantification data from S8::Mfn1 and S8::Mfn2 mice

claim: Mutant mitochondria had aberrant cristae morphology characterized by a fourfold reduction in the number of linear cristae elements and a fourfold increase in swollen, vesiculated cristae.
source: Mutant mitochondria had aberrant cristae morphology characterized by a fourfold reduction in the number of linear cristae elements and a fourfold increase in swollen, vesiculated cristae (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by 3D EM tomography data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: All vesiculated cristae in S8::Dm mitochondria could be traced back to the inner mitochondrial membrane using 3D EM tomography.
source: Despite their isolated appearance, all vesiculated cristae in S8::Dm mitochondria could be traced back to the inner mitochondrial membrane using 3D EM tomography (Video 4).
evidence: Supported by 3D EM tomography shown in Video 4

claim: Many cristae junctions (CJs) in mutant mitochondria are significantly widened in diameter.
source: Furthermore, many cristae junctions (CJs) in mutant mitochondria are significantly widened in diameter (Figure 5C and D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5C, D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: While most of the CJs in control spermatocytes are narrower than 22.5 nm (64%), the majority in S8::Dm are wider (78%).
source: While most of the CJs in control spermatocytes are narrower than 22.5 nm (64%), the majority in S8::Dm are wider (78%) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: S8::Dm sections show increased TUNEL-positive cells, indicative of cell death by apoptosis.
source: Indeed, S8::Dm sections show increased TUNEL-positive cells, indicative of cell death by apoptosis (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 5E and F

claim: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed two general categories of proteins that are significantly reduced in mitochondria from Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs: the mitochondrial respiratory chain and the mitochondrial ribosome.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed two general categories of proteins that are significantly reduced in mitochondria from Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs: the mitochondrial respiratory chain and the mitochondrial ribosome (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by SILAC proteomics data shown in Figure 6A and Supplementary file 1

claim: 31 out of 34 (91%) identified complex I subunits were reduced in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs.
source: Indeed, 31 out of 34 (91%) identified complex I subunits, all 12 (100%) complex IV subunits, and 74 out of 80 (93%) mitochondrial ribosomal subunits were reduced in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by SILAC proteomics data in Supplementary file 2

claim: All 12 (100%) complex IV subunits were reduced in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs.
source: Indeed, 31 out of 34 (91%) identified complex I subunits, all 12 (100%) complex IV subunits, and 74 out of 80 (93%) mitochondrial ribosomal subunits were reduced in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by SILAC proteomics data in Supplementary file 2

claim: 74 out of 80 (93%) mitochondrial ribosomal subunits were reduced in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs.
source: Indeed, 31 out of 34 (91%) identified complex I subunits, all 12 (100%) complex IV subunits, and 74 out of 80 (93%) mitochondrial ribosomal subunits were reduced in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by SILAC proteomics data in Supplementary file 2

claim: Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs had significantly lower levels of the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, MPC2.
source: Consistent with reduced OXPHOS activity, Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs had significantly lower levels of the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, MPC2 (Bricker et al., 2012; Vanderperre et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by SILAC proteomics data with citations to Bricker et al., 2012 and Vanderperre et al., 2016

claim: TFAM, a mitochondrial transcriptional activator and mtDNA packaging protein, was significantly reduced in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs.
source: Additionally, TFAM, a mitochondrial transcriptional activator and mtDNA packaging protein, was significantly reduced.
evidence: Supported by SILAC proteomics data

claim: 14 out of 18 (78%) complex I and IV assembly factors were increased in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs.
source: Intriguingly, 14 out of 18 (78%) complex I and IV assembly factors were increased in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs and of the seven that reached statistical significance, all were increased (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by SILAC proteomics data shown in Figure 6B

claim: 17 out of 21 (81%) detected mitochondrial import proteins were increased in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs.
source: 17 out of 21 (81%) detected mitochondrial import proteins were increased, and of the 10 that reached statistical significance, all were increased in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by SILAC proteomics data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Mitofusin knockdown in GC-2spd(ts) cells causes widespread mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: Strikingly, mitofusin knockdown in GCs causes widespread mitochondrial fragmentation and reduction in all OXPHOS subunits tested by western blotting: complex I subunit (NdufB8), complex II subunit SDHB, complex III subunit UQRC2, complex IV subunit MTCOI, and complex V subunit ATP5A (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A and B

claim: Mitofusin knockdown in GC-2spd(ts) cells causes reduction in all OXPHOS subunits tested by western blotting.
source: Strikingly, mitofusin knockdown in GCs causes widespread mitochondrial fragmentation and reduction in all OXPHOS subunits tested by western blotting: complex I subunit (NdufB8), complex II subunit SDHB, complex III subunit UQRC2, complex IV subunit MTCOI, and complex V subunit ATP5A (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C and D

claim: Mitofusin knockdown in GC-2spd(ts) cells caused a severe reduction in basal and maximal respiration, ATP production, and spare capacity.
source: Mitofusin knockdown caused a severe reduction in basal and maximal respiration, ATP production, and spare capacity (Figure 7E and F), but not glycolysis (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 7E, F, and G

claim: Mitofusin knockdown in GC-2spd(ts) cells did not affect glycolysis.
source: Mitofusin knockdown caused a severe reduction in basal and maximal respiration, ATP production, and spare capacity (Figure 7E and F), but not glycolysis (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 7G

claim: Mitofusin knockdown in MEFs caused mitochondrial fragmentation but not OXPHOS deficiency.
source: Interestingly, mitofusin knockdown in MEFs caused mitochondrial fragmentation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), but not OXPHOS deficiency (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and 3

claim: GC-2spd(ts) cells are particularly sensitive to loss of mitofusins.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that GCs are particularly sensitive to loss of mitofusins.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of GC and MEF responses to mitofusin knockdown

claim: Most spermatocytes in S8::Dm mice show a heterogeneous staining pattern in which a substantial subset of mito-Dendra2-positive mitochondria clearly lack OXPHOS components.
source: In contrast, most spermatocytes in S8::Dm mice show a heterogeneous staining pattern in which a substantial subset of mito-Dendra2-positive mitochondria clearly lack OXPHOS components.
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence analysis described in the text

claim: S8::Dm spermatocytes have reduced and heterogeneous expression of the complex I subunit NdufB6, the complex IV subunit MTCOI, and the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier MPC1.
source: Consistent with the proteomics in cultured cells, S8::Dm spermatocytes have reduced and heterogeneous expression of the complex I subunit NdufB6, the complex IV subunit MTCOI, and the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier MPC1 (an obligate binding partner of MPC2).
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence analysis

claim: The mtDNA-encoded MTCOI has the most heterogeneous expression in S8::Dm spermatocytes.
source: We noted that the mtDNA-encoded MTCOI has the most heterogeneous expression.
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence analysis

claim: Many shMfn1;Mfn2 GC-2spd(ts) cells display reduced or heterogeneous MTCOI expression, with a substantial subset of mitochondria lacking MTCOI.
source: Similarly, many shMfn1;Mfn2 GCs display reduced or heterogeneous MTCOI expression, with a substantial subset of mitochondria lacking MTCOI (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: There is mitochondrial heterogeneity in differentiated spermatogonia in S8::Dm mice.
source: In agreement with the progressive loss of differentiated spermatogonia in S8::Dm mice, there is also mitochondrial heterogeneity in this cell type (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2

claim: There is mitochondrial heterogeneity in undifferentiated spermatogonia in S8::Dm mice.
source: Surprisingly, we also find mitochondrial heterogeneity in undifferentiated spermatogonia, which are not depleted in S8::Dm mice.
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence analysis

claim: Undifferentiated spermatogonia can tolerate mitochondrial heterogeneity, suggesting that these cells are physiologically different.
source: However, the undifferentiated spermatogonia can apparently tolerate this defect, suggesting that these cells are physiologically different.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that undifferentiated spermatogonia are not depleted despite mitochondrial heterogeneity

claim: Spermatozoa isolated from S8::Mfn1 and S8::Mfn2 mice show reduction of both COX and SDH activities.
source: To test for functional changes in mitochondrial activity, we performed COX/SDH enzyme histochemistry on spermatozoa isolated from S8::Mfn1 and S8::Mfn2 mice and found reduction of both COX and SDH activities (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by COX/SDH enzyme histochemistry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3

claim: Fresh-frozen testis sections from S8::Dm mice show a severe reduction of COX and SDH activities in germ cells.
source: Because S8::Dm mice do not produce any sperm, we performed COX/SDH enzyme histochemistry in fresh-frozen testis sections and found a severe reduction of COX and SDH activities in S8::Dm germ cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by COX/SDH enzyme histochemistry data shown in Figure 8C

claim: Mitofusin depletion in germ cells in vivo causes ultrastructural defects, heterogeneity in OXPHOS expression, and reduced OXPHOS subunits and activity.
source: Thus, consistent with data in MEFs and immortalized spermatocytes, mitofusin depletion in germ cells in vivo causes ultrastructural defects, heterogeneity in OXPHOS expression, and reduced OXPHOS subunits and activity (Figure 9).
evidence: Summary conclusion supported by multiple lines of experimental data shown in Figure 9

claim: Spermatocytes require mitochondrial fusion as they undergo an acute upregulation of OXPHOS during MPI.
source: Our study reveals that spermatocytes require mitochondrial fusion as they undergo an acute upregulation of OXPHOS during MPI (Figure 9).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 9

claim: Mfn1 but not Mfn2 is essential for the metabolic transition during MPI.
source: Analysis of the single mutant mice showed that Mfn1 but not Mfn2 is essential for this transition.
evidence: Based on comparison of S8::Mfn1 and S8::Mfn2 phenotypes

claim: The metabolic transition during MPI coincides with increased mitochondrial density, mitochondrial elongation, and upregulation of OXPHOS activity.
source: We show that this transition coincides with increased mitochondrial density, mitochondrial elongation, and upregulation of OXPHOS activity, which are all blocked in fusion-deficient spermatocytes.
evidence: Based on experimental observations of mitochondrial changes during MPI

claim: The increased OXPHOS in pachytene spermatocytes is likely required to fuel ATP-consuming biochemical reactions involved in homologous recombination and DSB repair.
source: The increased OXPHOS in pachytene spermatocytes is likely required to fuel ATP-consuming biochemical reactions involved in homologous recombination and DSB repair.
evidence: Speculation based on the metabolic requirements of meiotic processes

claim: Spermatocytes switch their energy dependence from glucose to lactate and pyruvate as they traverse the blood-testis barrier.
source: As a result, spermatocytes switch their energy dependence from glucose to lactate and pyruvate, which are preferred substrates for OXPHOS (Bajpai et al., 1998; Grootegoed et al., 1984; Nakamura et al., 1984; Rato et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Round spherical mitochondria with orthodox cristae in early MPI convert in pachytene to more elongated mitochondria with condensed cristae.
source: Round spherical mitochondria with orthodox cristae in early MPI convert in pachytene to more elongated mitochondria with condensed cristae (De Martino et al., 1979; Meinhardt, 1999; Seitz et al., 1995), an ultrastructure associated with active OXPHOS (Hackenbrock, 1966; Mannella, 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Mitofusins are required not only in spermatocytes, but also in differentiating spermatogonia.
source: In contrast to the Mfn1 study (Zhang et al., 2016), we show that mitofusins are required not only in spermatocytes, but also in differentiating spermatogonia (Figure 9).
evidence: Based on experimental data showing depletion of differentiating spermatogonia, shown in Figure 9

claim: S8::Mfn1, S8::Mfn2, and S8::Dm mice exhibit a progressive loss of all differentiated germ cell types, including the differentiating spermatogonia that give rise to spermatocytes.
source: S8::Mfn1, S8::Mfn2, and S8::Dm mice exhibit a progressive loss of all differentiated germ cell types, including the differentiating spermatogonia that give rise to spermatocytes.
evidence: Based on experimental observations in adult mice

claim: The age-dependent loss of germ cells is likely caused by the progressive depletion of mitofusin gene products due to the iterative nature of spermatogenesis.
source: The age-dependent loss is likely caused by the progressive depletion of mitofusin gene products due to the iterative nature of spermatogenesis.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation of progressive phenotype worsening with age

claim: At P24, during the first round of spermatogenesis, germ cells may contain residual levels of mitofusin activity sufficient to mitigate effects on spermatogonia.
source: At P24, during the first round of spermatogenesis, germ cells may contain residual levels of mitofusin activity sufficient to mitigate effects on spermatogonia.
evidence: Speculation to explain the difference between P24 and P56 phenotypes

claim: Undifferentiated spermatogonia, differentiating spermatogonia, and spermatocytes show progressively increasing requirements for mitochondrial fusion.
source: Undifferentiated spermatogonia, differentiating spermatogonia, and spermatocytes therefore show progressively increasing requirements for mitochondrial fusion.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the differential sensitivity of germ cell types to mitofusin loss

claim: These results are consistent with a paradigm in various stem cell systems, wherein stem cells compared with differentiated cells are less dependent on mitochondrial OXPHOS.
source: These results are consistent with a paradigm in various (but not all) stem cell systems, wherein stem cells compared with differentiated cells are less dependent on mitochondrial OXPHOS (Chen and Chan, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen and Chan, 2017

claim: The two major phenotypes of S8::Dm mice—meiotic failure and spermatogonial differentiation—are also observed with loss of Mfn1 alone.
source: The two major phenotypes of S8::Dm mice—meiotic failure and spermatogonial differentiation—are also observed with loss of Mfn1 alone.
evidence: Based on experimental observations in S8::Mfn1 mice

claim: The spermatogenesis defects should be attributed to loss of mitochondrial fusion, rather than non-fusion functions like ER-mitochondria tethering that have been attributed to Mfn2.
source: This observation suggests that these defects should be attributed to loss of mitochondrial fusion, rather than non-fusion functions, like ER-mitochondria tethering, that have been attributed to Mfn2 (de Brito and Scorrano, 2008).
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that Mfn1 loss alone recapitulates the phenotype, with citation to de Brito and Scorrano, 2008

claim: Full inhibition of mitochondrial fusion by deletion of both mitofusins uncovers their role in maintaining the respiratory chain and mitochondrial translation.
source: In our study, full inhibition of mitochondrial fusion by deletion of both mitofusins uncovers their role in maintaining the respiratory chain and mitochondrial translation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SILAC proteomics data

claim: The increase in respiratory chain complex I and IV assembly factors and mitochondrial import proteins in Mfn1/Mfn2-null MEFs may be indicative of a compensatory stress response to the cellular dysfunction caused by mitochondrial fusion deficiency.
source: These increases may be indicative of a compensatory stress response to the cellular dysfunction caused by mitochondrial fusion deficiency.
evidence: Speculation to explain the observed increase in assembly factors and import proteins

claim: The metabolic derangements revealed by proteomics in MEFs extend to a spermatocyte cell line and to spermatocytes in vivo.
source: Importantly, the metabolic derangements revealed by proteomics in MEFs extend to a spermatocyte cell line and to spermatocytes in vivo.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of MEF, GC, and in vivo data

claim: Mitochondrial fusion safeguards mitochondrial function and male fertility.
source: Thus, our findings provide a rationale for how mitochondrial fusion safeguards mitochondrial function and male fertility.
evidence: Overall conclusion drawn from all experimental findings
